θεὶς τὴν περὶ αὐτοῦ διάθεσιν δείκνυσιν· εἶτα εἰπὼν ἵνα καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν
συμβασιλεύσωμεν, ἐμφαίνει ὅτι τὰ ἐκείνων κατορθώματα ἴδια λογίζεται ἀγαθά. οὐκ
ἀπεικὸς καὶ ὡς ἐν ἐρωτήσει ἀναγινώσκειν τὸ ἐβασιλεύσατε καὶ ἐπλουτήσατε, ἵνα ᾖ
ἐν ἤθει τὰ εἰρημένα τῷ ἤδη κεKorασμένοι ἐστέ. 1 Kor 4,9Ὡς ὁρῶ γάρ, ἐὰν ὑμεῖς
ἐπλουτήσατε καὶ ἐβασιλεύσατε χωρὶς ἡμῶν, ἡμεῖς ἔσχατοι καὶ ἐπιθανάτιοι
γεγόναμεν οἱ πάντα ὑποστάντες. Ἀνθρώποις μέν, φησίν, ὡς ὁρῶσι τὰ ἡμέτερα κακά,
ἀγγελικοῖς δὲ ὡς θαυμάζουσι τὰς ἡμετέρας ἐνστάσεις. 1 Kor 4,10Ὅμοια καὶ ταῦτα. οἱ
διδάσκοντες ὑμᾶς ἐν καταφρονήσει καὶ εὐτελείᾳ ὡς καὶ μωροὶ νομίζεσθαι τῷ κόσμῳ,
ὑμεῖς δὲ οἱ διδασκόμενοι ἐν πλούτῳ ἤδη καὶ τιμαῖς Χριστοῦ εἶναι βούλεσθε. ταῦτα δὲ
λέγει 241 1 Kor 4,8– δεικνὺς ὅτι ἐν τοῖς πνευματικοῖς χαρίσμασιν οὐκ ἔστι μαθητὴς
ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον. 1 Kor 4,11–13Ἡμεῖς πάντα διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ὑπομένομεν καὶ
μέχρι νῦν ταπεινοῦμεν ἑαυτούς. καὶ πῶς δυνατὸν ὑμᾶς ἐν σαρκὶ ζῶντας προτιμᾶσθαι
παρὰ θεῷ τῶν καμνόντων, τῶν διωκομένων, τῶν λοιδορουμένων, τῶν
κολαφιζομένων; παιδεύει δὲ διὰ πάντων τούτων πῶς δεῖ τὸν Χριστιανὸν εἶναι καὶ
ταπεινοῦν ἑαυτόν.Ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀποψήγματα. ὥσπερ ἀποσαρώματα καὶ κόπρος ἐξ οἴκου
ἀποκαθαρθέντος ληφθεῖσα γεγόναμεν, ἀπὸ πάντων εὐτελιζόμενοι, καί ἐσμεν
πάντων ἀποκαθάρματα πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ὑποτιθέντες ἑαυτοὺς διὰ Χριστόν.
περίψημα δὲ λέγεται τὸ σάβανον ὃ τοὺς ἱδρώτας τοῦ κάμνοντος ἀποψήχει καὶ
ἀπομάσσεται τὴν κάκωσιν τὴν ἐπικειμένην. 1 Kor 4,14Ἰσχυρῶς διὰ τῶν πρώτων
καθαψάμενος διὰ τούτων παραμυθεῖται, ἵνα διὰ τῶν στυπτικῶν καὶ γλυκέων κεράσῃ
τῆς σωτηρίας τὴν δύναμιν. ἐντρέπων, διατρέπων. 1 Kor 4,15 Εἰπὼν ἑαυτὸν πατέρα,
ἐκείνους δὲ παιδαγωγοὺς ἀφ' ὧν ἐκαλοῦντο, δείκνυσιν ὅτι γνησιωτέραν ἔχει τῶν
ἄλλων περὶ αὐτοὺς διάθεσιν, καὶ ὡς ὑπὸ πατρὸς νουθετούμενοι ἀγανακτεῖν οὐκ
ὀφείλουσιν. 1 Kor 4,16Ἐν τῷ μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν τινων καὶ ἐπαίρεσθαι μιμηταί μου
γίνεσθε, καὶ ἐν τῷ μὴ ἀπό τινος καλεῖσθαι ἀλλ' ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ. 1 Kor 4,18–Ὁρᾷς ὅτι
ἐκεῖνα τὰ λεγόμενα αὐτῷ, τὸ ἡμεῖς ἀσθενεῖς, ὑμεῖς δυνατοί, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα, πρὸς
τὸ πεφυσιῶσθαί τινας 242 ἐλέγετο καὶ ἐπῆρθαι. Ἐλεύσομαι δὲ ταχέως πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν
ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ, καὶ γνώσομαι οὐ τὸν λόγον τῶν πεφυσιωμένων ἀλλὰ τὴν δύναμιν.
δι' ὧν φησιν καὶ ἐλέγχει ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ μαρτυρεῖ αὐτὸς ἐπιτηδειότητα πρὸς
ἐπανόρθωσιν τῷ τὴν παρουσίαν ἑαυτοῦ ἀπειλεῖν· ὡς γὰρ εἰ φανείη ταπεινουμένων,
ἐπαγγέλλεται τὴν παρουσίαν, τῷ λόγῳ πρὸ τῆς παρουσίας διορθούμενος. πλὴν ἀλλὰ
προσέθηκε τὸ ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ· ὑπὸ μὲν τῆς ἀγανακτήσεως ἠπείχθη εἰπεῖν ὅτι
ἐλεύσομαι, ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς εὐλαβείας ὑπεμνήσθη προσθεῖναι τὴν καλλίστην προσθήκην
τὴν ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θέλῃ ἐνταῦθα δὲ ὃ πρότερον ἐπεσκιασμένως ἔλεγεν ἵνα μὴ δόξῃ
σφοδρῶς ἐλέγχειν, ἀνακαλύπτει· οὐ γὰρ ἐν λόγῳ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ, δηλονότι τῷ
εὐπαιδεύτῳ· οὐ γὰρ ἄνευ λόγου ἐδίδασκον οἱ ἀπόστολοι καὶ ἐκήρυττον. 241,ξολ2
∆ῆλον καὶ ἐκ τούτων ὅτι τὸ ἡ μεῖς ἀσθενεῖς, ὑμεῖς δὲ δυνατοί, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πρὸς
πεφυσιῶσθαί τινας ἐλέγετο. 242,ξολ2Ἐπαγγέλλεται τὴν παρουσίαν αὐτοῦ, ὅπως ἐὰν
φθάσωσιν ἑαυτοὺς διορθώσασθαι. διὰ μὲν οὖν τὴν ἀγανάκτησιν ἠναγκάσθη εἰπεῖν
τὸ ἐλεύσομαι, διὰ δὲ τὴν εὐλάβειαν προσέθηκεν τὸ ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ. Σαφέστερον
καὶ ἐκ τούτων ἐγένετο ὅτι πρὸς τοὺς μεγαλαυχοῦντας ἐπὶ τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ κόσμου
τούτου ἀγανακτεῖ· οὐ γὰρ τὸν κοινὸν βούλεται διαβάλλειν λόγον. τοῦτο δὲ καὶ
αὐτοῖς εἰς πάντας ἐκήρυσσεν. 1 Kor 4,21Ἐπειδὴ διττή ἐστιν ἡ ἐπανόρθωσις, πῆ μὲν
διὰ νουθεσίας τοῖς πειθηνίοις, πῆ δὲ διὰ βίας καὶ ἀνάγκης τοῖς σκληροτραχήλοις,
φιλανθρώπως τούτων τὴν αἵρεσιν ἐπ' αὐτοῖς πεποίηκεν, ὅπως ἀναμετανοοῦντες
ἑαυτοὺς διορθώσονται. ῥάβδον δὲ εἶπεν τὴν ἀναγκαστικὴν τοῦ πνεύματος δύναμιν,
ᾗ ἐχρήσατο Παῦλος κατὰἘλύμα καὶ κατ' αὐτοῦ τοῦ Παύλου ὁ θεός. 1 Kor 5,1–5 Οὐκ
ἐπειδὴ γυναῖκα τὸν εἰρημένον τρόπον εἶχεν ἐκεῖνος, ἀλλ' 243 ὅτι ἐλλόγιμος ἦν, καὶ
οὐχὶ ἐπένθουν ὅτι γυναῖκα τοῦ πατρὸς εἶχεν, ἀλλ' ἐπεφυσίωντο ὅτι εὐπαίδευτος ἦν·
τὸ γὰρ πένθος αὐτῶν ἢ ἐχώριζε τὸν πορνεύσαντα ἐπιμένοντα, ἢ τοῦ πράγματος τὴν
ἀτοπίαν ἐξώριζεν καὶ ἐπανῆγεν αὐτόν. Οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἐργασάμενον ἀλλὰ
κατεργασάμενον· οὐ γὰρ συναρπασθεὶς ἔπεσεν, ἀλλ' ἔργῳ ἐχρήσατο τῷ κακῷ. καὶ
πνεύματι δὲ παρεῖναι λέγει συνψηφιζόμενος καὶ συνκατακρίνων– πνεῦμα δὲ τὸ
pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: and the 'would that indeed' in between) placing, he shows the disposition about himself; then saying 'so that we also might reign with you', he makes evident that he reckons their achievements his own goods. Not unlikely also to read as in a question 'you reigned' and 'you became rich', so that the things said may be in character with 'already you are sated'. [Label 1 Cor 4:9.] For as I see, if you became rich and reigned without us, we have become last and condemned to death, we who underwent all things. 'To men', he says, as seeing our evils, 'and to angelic (beings)', as marvelling at our steadfastness. [Label 1 Cor 4:10.] These too are similar. Those teaching you (are) in contempt and cheapness so as even to be thought fools by the world, but you the taught wish to be already in wealth and honours of Christ. And he says these things [page 241; stray label 1 Kor 4,8-] showing that in the spiritual gifts there is no disciple above the teacher (Matt 10:24). [Label 1 Cor 4:11-13.] We endure all things because of Christ and until now humble ourselves. And how is it possible that you, living in flesh, are preferred with God to those toiling, being persecuted, being reviled, being beaten? And he educates through all these how the Christian must be and humble himself. Instead of 'scrapings'. As sweepings and dung taken from a cleaned house we have become, cheapened by all, and we are offscourings of all, subjecting ourselves to all men because of Christ. And 'peripsema' is called the towel which wipes off the sweats of the one toiling and wipes away the affliction lying on (him). [Label 1 Cor 4:14.] Having fastened on (them) strongly through the first things, through these he consoles, so that through the astringent and sweet things he may mix the power of salvation. 'Shaming': confounding. [Label 1 Cor 4:15.] Having called himself father, and those from whom they were called tutors, he shows that he has a more genuine disposition toward them than the others, and that being admonished as by a father they ought not to be indignant. [Label 1 Cor 4:16.] In not despising some and being lifted up become imitators of me, and in not being called from anyone but from Christ. [Label 1 Cor 4:18- (open).] You see that those things said by him, 'we weak, you strong', and all the others, were said toward some having been puffed up [page 242] and lifted up. 'But I will come quickly to you, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the word of those puffed up but the power.' Through which (words) he both refutes strongly and himself testifies (their) suitability for correction by threatening his presence; for as if it might appear (that they are) being humbled, he announces the presence, correcting by word before the presence. But yet he added 'if the Lord wills': by the indignation he was urged to say 'I will come', but by the reverence he was reminded to add the finest addition 'if the Lord wills'. And here what he said before in a shadowed way, so as not to seem to refute vehemently, he uncovers: 'for the kingdom of God (is) not in word', clearly the well-educated (word); for the apostles did not teach and preach without word. [Second column, pages 241-242, parallel:] It is clear also from these that 'we weak, you strong' and the other things were said toward some having been puffed up. He announces his presence, so that they may get ahead in correcting themselves. So because of the indignation he was compelled to say 'I will come', and because of the reverence he added 'if the Lord wills'. More clearly also from these it became (evident) that he is indignant toward those boasting greatly over the wisdom of this world; for he does not wish to slander the common word. And this he also proclaimed to them, to all. [Label 1 Cor 4:21.] Since correction is twofold, in one way through admonition for the obedient, in another through force and necessity for the stiff-necked, kindly he made the choice of these (rest) on them, so that repenting they will correct themselves. And he called rod the compelling power of the Spirit, which Paul used against Elymas (Acts 13:8-11), and God against Paul himself (Acts 9:3-9). [Label 1 Cor 5:1-5.] Not because that man had a woman in the stated way, but [page 243] because he was eloquent; and they did not mourn that he had his father's wife, but were puffed up that he was well-educated; for their mourning either would separate the one who fornicated, (if) persisting, or would banish the absurdity of the matter and bring him back. Not simply having done but having worked out (accomplished): for he did not fall being snatched away, but used the evil as a work. And he says (he is) present in spirit, voting together and condemning together - and spirit (… continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: …he shows how he himself feels. Then, by saying "so that we too might reign with you," he makes plain that he counts their successes as blessings of his own. It is reasonable, too, to read "you have reigned" and "you have become rich" as questions, so that the words carry the same tone as "Already you are filled."

On 1 Corinthians 4:9: As I see it, if you have become rich and have reigned without us, then we who have endured everything have become the last of all, men condemned to death. "To men," he says, because they see our sufferings, "and to angels," because they marvel at our steadfastness.

On 1 Corinthians 4:10: These words are of the same kind. Those who teach you live in contempt and poverty, so that the world even takes them for fools, while you who are taught want to be already in wealth and in the honors of Christ. He says this to show that in spiritual gifts "a disciple is not above his teacher" (Matthew 10:24).

On 1 Corinthians 4:11–13: We endure everything for Christ's sake, and to this day we humble ourselves. How then can you, living in the flesh, be preferred before God to those who toil, are persecuted, are reviled and are beaten? Through all this he teaches what a Christian must be like, and how he must humble himself. That is, scrapings. We have become like the sweepings and the dung carried out of a house that has been cleaned, despised by everyone, and we are the refuse of all, putting ourselves beneath everyone for Christ's sake. And "offscouring" is the word for the towel that wipes the sweat off a laborer and rubs away the grime that clings to him.

On 1 Corinthians 4:14: Having attacked them hard in the earlier words, he comforts them with these, so that by mixing the astringent with the sweet he may make up a medicine with the power to save. "Shaming" means putting to confusion.

On 1 Corinthians 4:15: By calling himself their father, and the men they were named after their tutors, he shows that his affection for them is truer than the others', and that, since a father is the one warning them, they ought not to take offense.
On 1 Corinthians 4:16: Become imitators of me by not looking down on anyone or being lifted up, and by being called after no one but Christ.

On 1 Corinthians 4:18–20: You see that what he said earlier, "We are weak, but you are strong," and all the rest, was said because some had become puffed up and proud. "But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power." In these words he rebukes them strongly, and by threatening to come in person he himself bears witness that they can still be set right. He announces his coming as if to see whether they will show themselves humbled, and corrects them by his word before he comes. Yet he added "if the Lord wills." Indignation drove him to say "I will come," but reverence reminded him to add that finest of additions, "if the Lord wills." Here he brings into the open what he had said earlier in veiled terms, so as not to seem to rebuke them too harshly: "for the kingdom of God is not in word," meaning polished speech, since the apostles did not teach and preach without words.

The second catena form adds: He announces his coming so that they may set themselves right before he arrives. It becomes clearer from this that his anger is aimed at those who boast in the wisdom of this world, for he does not mean to discredit ordinary speech; and this he proclaimed to them too, for all to hear.

On 1 Corinthians 4:21: Correction comes in two forms: by admonition for those who will listen, and by force and compulsion for the stiff-necked. In his kindness he left the choice between them to the Corinthians, so that they might repent and set themselves right. By "rod" he meant the compelling power of the Spirit, which Paul used against Elymas (Acts 13:8–11), and which God used against Paul himself (Acts 9:3–9).

On 1 Corinthians 5:1–5: They were puffed up, not because that man had a woman in the way described, but because he was eloquent. They did not mourn that he had his father's wife; they were proud that he was well educated. Their mourning would either have cut the fornicator off if he persisted, or driven the outrage out and brought him back. Not simply "who did" but "who has carried out": he did not fall because he was swept away; he made the evil his deliberate work. And he says that he is present in spirit, casting his vote with them and joining in the condemnation (by "spirit" he means…

choices.english: collapsed; new sentences printed after 'The second catena form adds:'
choices.why: Second form of the 4:18-20 note. 'so that they may set themselves right before he arrives', the remark on the wisdom of this world, and 'this he proclaimed to them too' have no counterpart; the rest repeats the first form.
The edition's label is open-ended; the note quotes 4:19 and 4:20, so the range is closed by the lemmas it quotes.
